title: A cold lookup, and why you almost never pay for one

spec.title: A cold lookup, and why you almost never pay for one
spec.description: Resolution walks a hierarchy — root, TLD, authoritative — but caching at every layer means most lookups never leave the machine.

nodes.label: TTL is the dial
nodes.sublabel:
Long: fewer lookups, slow changes.
Short: fast failover, more queries.
Lower it a DAY before a migration —
the change only takes effect after
the OLD TTL expires.

steps.text: Nothing is cached anywhere, so the query reaches the recursive resolver, whose job is to do the walking on the client's behalf.
The root servers do not know the answer — they know who is responsible for .com.
The .com servers likewise do not know the address; they know which nameservers are authoritative for example.com.

The authoritative server returns the record with a TTL. Several round trips have elapsed — a cold resolution can run past 100 ms, which is why DNS shows up in first-visit page-load waterfalls and vanishes afterwards.
The browser, the OS, or the resolver already holds the record within its TTL and answers immediately. The hierarchy above is never touched — which is why DNS feels free.

That cache lifetime was set once, here, by the authoritative server. It is the only lever you have over how long a stale answer can survive — and it means a change you make is invisible to anyone still holding a cached record.

Because you control the answer, you control the routing: return the nearest region's address, weight traffic by percentage for a gradual migration, or stop returning an address that fails its health check.

But TTLs are advisory. Some resolvers apply their own minimums and some applications cache a resolved address for the process lifetime. Treat DNS as eventually consistent and put a health-checked load balancer in front of anything that must move in seconds.
